options.content: an illness that lasts a long time and usually develops slowly
options.rationale: Correct: chronic means long-lasting.

options.content: an illness that spreads quickly from one person to another through contact
options.rationale: This describes an infectious disease.

options.content: an illness that lasts only a day or two
options.rationale: Short illnesses are called acute.

options.content: an illness caused only by an injury
options.rationale: Injuries are not chronic illnesses.

explanation: Chronic illnesses last months, years or for life, such as diabetes and hypertension.

options.content: high blood pressure
options.rationale: Correct: hyper = too high; tension = pressure.

options.content: high blood sugar
options.rationale: High blood sugar is the sign of diabetes.

options.content: a lung infection
options.rationale: Hypertension affects blood pressure, not the lungs.

options.content: a lack of iron in the blood
options.rationale: This is a form of anaemia.

explanation: Hypertension is blood pressure that stays too high over a long time.

stem: Why is hypertension often called a "silent killer"?

options.content: Many people have no symptoms until serious damage is done
options.rationale: Correct: it can go unnoticed for years.

options.content: It spreads silently from person to person
options.rationale: Hypertension is not infectious.

options.content: It affects only people who do not speak much
options.rationale: It has nothing to do with speech.

options.content: It always kills within a few days of the first symptoms appearing
options.rationale: It develops slowly over years.

explanation: Hypertension often has no symptoms, so regular blood pressure checks are important.

stem: Which of these is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes that a person **can change**?

options.content: growing older
options.rationale: Age cannot be changed.

options.content: having a parent with diabetes
options.rationale: Family history cannot be changed.

options.content: being born in a particular year
options.rationale: This cannot be changed.

options.content: physical inactivity
options.rationale: Correct: a person can become more active.

explanation: Diet, activity, weight, tobacco and alcohol can be changed; age and family history cannot.

stem: Which statement about chronic illnesses such as diabetes is correct?

options.content: They are caught by sharing cups, plates and towels with a sick person
options.rationale: Diabetes is not infectious.

options.content: They affect only people living in towns
options.rationale: Rural people are also affected.

options.content: They can be cured by any herbal remedy
options.rationale: No herb has been shown to cure diabetes.

options.content: They cannot be passed from one person to another
options.rationale: Correct: they are non-communicable.

explanation: Most chronic illnesses are non-communicable; they affect people everywhere and need care from health workers.

stem: Themba's uncle has hypertension. Which change to his diet would **most** help to control it?

options.content: eating more salty snacks
options.rationale: This would raise blood pressure further.

options.content: eating less salt
options.rationale: Correct: too much salt raises blood pressure.

options.content: drinking more sugary fizzy drinks
options.rationale: Sugary drinks add weight and raise other risks.

options.content: eating fewer vegetables
options.rationale: Vegetables are part of a healthy diet.

explanation: Cutting salt is one of the most important diet changes for people with high blood pressure, alongside treatment.
hints: Which ingredient is most linked to blood pressure?

stem: A clinic offers free blood pressure and blood sugar checks to adults who feel well. What is this called?

options.content: vaccination
options.rationale: Vaccines protect against infectious diseases.

options.content: quarantine
options.rationale: Quarantine separates people who may be infectious.

options.content: screening
options.rationale: Correct: testing people who feel well to find disease early.

options.content: contact tracing
options.rationale: This finds people exposed to an infectious disease.

explanation: Screening finds illnesses early, when they are easier to control.
hints: The people tested have no symptoms yet.

stem: Which explanation **best** accounts for rising rates of type 2 diabetes in many towns?

options.content: Diabetes is spread by contaminated water in towns
options.rationale: Diabetes is not water-borne.

options.content: Diets with more sugar and fat, combined with less physical activity
options.rationale: Correct: lifestyle changes raise the risk.

options.content: Town clinics give people diabetes when they test them
options.rationale: Testing finds diabetes; it does not cause it.

options.content: People in towns eat more vegetables and walk more than people elsewhere
options.rationale: This would lower the risk.

explanation: Processed, sugary and fatty food and less walking increase overweight and diabetes risk.
hints: Compare town diets and transport with those of earlier generations.

stem: Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot control the level of sugar in the blood.
explanation: True. The body makes too little insulin or cannot use it properly.

stem: A person who feels better should stop taking their blood pressure medicine without asking a health worker.
explanation: False. Medicines must be taken as prescribed; feeling well often means the treatment is working.

stem: Match each chronic illness with a possible complication if it is not controlled.

right.content: wounds on the feet that do not heal

explanation: Diabetes damages nerves and blood vessels in the feet; hypertension can cause stroke; asthma can cause severe breathing attacks. Cholera is an infectious disease.

payload.template: Diseases that cannot be passed from person to person are called {{blank:a}} diseases. World Diabetes Day is marked on 14 {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Chronic illnesses are usually non-communicable (NCDs); World Diabetes Day is 14 November.

stem: State **four** risk factors for chronic illnesses such as diabetes and hypertension.

points.description: Any one of: unhealthy diet (salt, sugar, fat), physical inactivity, overweight, tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, stress, age, family history
A second different risk factor
A third different risk factor
A fourth different risk factor

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Too much salt and sugar in the diet, lack of exercise, smoking and family history.

explanation: One mark per correct risk factor.

stem: Explain **three** ways in which a chronic illness affects a family.

points.description: Identifies cost of treatment
Develops: money for transport, tests and medicines every month for years
Identifies burden of care
Develops: relatives (often women and girls) spend time caring, missing work or school
Identifies loss of income if a breadwinner cannot work / dies
Develops: the family's standard of living falls; children may leave school

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The family must pay for transport to the clinic, tests and medicines every month, often for many years. Relatives, often women and girls, spend time caring for the sick person and may miss work or school. If the sick person is a breadwinner who can no longer work, the family loses income and its standard of living falls.

explanation: One mark for each effect and one for its development.
hints: Think of money, time and income.

stem: Suggest **two** ways a school could help its learners reduce their risk of chronic illness later in life, and explain how each would help.

points.description: Suggests regular physical activity / sport for all learners
Explains that exercise builds lifelong habits and keeps weight healthy
Suggests healthy food in the tuck shop/dining hall / health education / anti-tobacco and alcohol clubs
Explains how it reduces a named risk factor

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The school could make sure every learner takes part in sport or physical activity several times a week, which builds a habit of exercise and helps keep weight healthy. It could also sell fruit and water in the tuck shop instead of fizzy drinks and salty snacks, so learners eat less sugar and salt.

explanation: One mark for each suitable suggestion and one for its explanation.
hints: Link each suggestion to a risk factor.

stem:
**Source A** — results of a fictional health survey of 200 adults in one ward (invented for this question)

> | Habit | Number of adults (out of 200) |
> |---|---|
> | Add salt to food at the table | 120 |
> | Do less than 30 minutes of exercise a day | 140 |
> | Smoke tobacco | 30 |
> | Have had a blood pressure check in the past year | 50 |

Study Source A and answer the questions. (The figures are invented for this question.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which risk factor was reported by the **largest** number of adults?

options.content: adding salt at the table
options.rationale: 120 adults, fewer than 140.

options.content: smoking tobacco
options.rationale: 30 adults.

options.content: too little exercise
options.rationale: Correct: 140 adults.

options.content: having a blood pressure check
options.rationale: This is screening, not a risk factor.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate how many adults had **not** had a blood pressure check in the past year, and state why this is a concern.

points.description: Hypertension often has no symptoms, so many cases may go undetected

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: 150 adults had not been checked. This is a concern because hypertension often has no symptoms, so many people may have it without knowing.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest how the ward could use these results to reduce chronic illness.

points.description: Targets the biggest risk factors shown (exercise, salt)
Suggests a practical action, e.g. walking or sports clubs, cooking demonstrations with less salt
Suggests increasing screening, e.g. free blood pressure checks at gatherings or the clinic

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The ward should focus on the most common risks: lack of exercise and salt. It could start community walking and sports groups and hold cooking demonstrations showing tasty meals with less salt. It could also arrange free blood pressure checks at markets, churches and meetings, because most adults have not been checked.

explanation: A data-based practice item on risk factors and screening.
hints: In (c), let the biggest numbers guide your suggestions.

stem: This question is about preventing chronic illnesses.

points.description: Way 1, e.g. eating less salt / a balanced diet
Described: how it lowers blood pressure or the risk
Way 2, e.g. regular exercise, healthy weight, no tobacco, no alcohol abuse, screening
Described: how it lowers blood pressure or the risk

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Eating less salt and more vegetables and fruit helps keep blood pressure normal. Regular exercise such as walking strengthens the heart and helps keep a healthy weight, which lowers blood pressure.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Preventing chronic illness is the responsibility of the individual, not the government." Discuss.

points.description: Individual responsibility: diet, exercise, tobacco, alcohol, going for screening, taking treatment
Government role: clinics, screening, medicines, health education, rules on tobacco/alcohol, healthy school food
Limits on individual choice: cost of healthy food, lack of safe places to exercise, lack of information; others (families, schools, churches) also matter
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Individuals have a large part to play. Most risk factors are about daily choices: what we eat, whether we exercise, whether we smoke or drink too much, and whether we go for check-ups and take treatment.

The government also has an important role. It runs clinics, offers screening and medicines, educates the public and can make rules, for example on selling alcohol and tobacco to young people.

Individual choice also has limits. Healthy food can be expensive, some areas have no safe places to exercise, and many people do not know their blood pressure because screening is not near them. Families, schools and churches also shape habits.

I disagree with the statement. Individuals must make healthy choices, but they can only do so when the government and communities make healthy choices possible and affordable.

explanation: A practice evaluative item on responsibility for preventing chronic illness.
hints: In (b), ask whether everyone is equally able to make healthy choices.
